key_facts: Nvidia reported quarterly revenue of $115.8 billion and profit of $65.3 billion for the three months ending in October, both above Wall Street expectations; revenue topped $100 billion for the first time, more than twice the year-earlier level. The company projected current-quarter revenue of about $130 billion.

Chief executive Jensen Huang resigned a week before the report after revelations of relationships violating the company's code of conduct, including one with a Chinese businesswoman U.S. intelligence determined was feeding information to Beijing; he also misled the board. Board chair Harvey C. Jones said there are no plans to reinstate him. Colette Kress is interim CEO; an independent investigation and a search for a new leader are underway.

Nvidia said it would stop shipping chips to China. Chinese sales in the reported quarter were about $2.4 billion, a small fraction of total revenue. The H200 export approval was granted under a deal with President Trump giving the U.S. government a 25 percent cut of China sales, but China has shown little interest in buying them.

Within the Trump administration, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has taken a softer line on Nvidia chip controls than most senior officials, who favor tighter restrictions; U.S. officials are pushing new restrictions on advanced AI chip sales.
importance_reason: Mega-cap earnings with a large beat and a guidance raise, combined with a CEO exit and new export-control pressure, have systemic relevance for the AI chip sector and US-China tech policy.
market_link: Nvidia's results and guidance shape sentiment across AI equities and semiconductor supply chains; new US chip export restrictions could affect Nvidia's China revenue and Southeast Asian AI investment, and the results are seen as setting the tone for Anthropic's IPO.

key_facts: The UK government backed the Milburn review, proposing sweeping reforms and spending billions on tailored support for under-25s not in employment, education or training (Neets), partly funded by cuts to some benefits; the report claims 440,000 young people could get jobs by 2036.

The Milburn report (250 pages) proposes a new 'youth allowance' at the basic Universal Credit rate for under-25s, ending the health top-up of Universal Credit and Personal Independence Payments (Pip) for that age group, and reduced employer National Insurance costs for 21- to 24-year-olds starting in retail and hospitality.

The report calls for around £5.8bn in total by 2036-37 on extra mental health and employment support, with an initial £500m to 'kickstart the reform programme' next year from repriotising existing spending; savings of £200m a year are assumed only from 2036/37, when the Neet share is projected to fall from 13% to 5%.

Draft welfare reform proposals are to be published early next year, with legislation to follow; the PM said a full government response would come next month after a separate Pip report by Sir Stephen Timms.

Opposition and internal critics: Kemi Badenoch agreed with the diagnosis but blamed Labour's rise in employer National Insurance and the youth minimum wage; some left-wing Labour MPs and Unison warned cuts to health-related benefits could push young people into poverty.
importance_reason: Major domestic social-policy and fiscal proposal with multi-billion spending implications, but no direct market-moving event (no rate decision, budget vote or price shock).
market_link: Multi-billion-pound fiscal commitments and changes to employer National Insurance costs could affect UK public finances and gilt sentiment, and lower youth employment costs for retail and hospitality firms; the effect is indirect and uncertain.

key_facts: Japan's exports in October surged 20.5% year on year, snapping a two-month slowdown; September was revised to 16.5%. Exports growth beat the 20% forecast of economists polled by Reuters.
Semiconductor equipment shipments jumped 49.7% by value; motor vehicle exports climbed 19.9%. Shipments to China rose 13.3% and to the U.S. rose 23.9%.

Import growth came in at 21.6%, sharply below the 25.8% analyst estimate. Petroleum imports rose 60.5% by value while volumes slipped 0.7%; imports from the U.S. jumped over 1,100% by value and 738% by volume, while Middle East shipments fell 16.5% by volume.
Japan's Q3 GDP surprisingly contracted 0.1% annualized. After the data, the Nikkei 225 rose 0.91% and the yen traded at 159.50 per dollar.
importance_reason: Strong export beat and a surprise GDP contraction matter for Japanese macro and the yen, but the data is a single monthly release without a policy decision or systemic shock.
market_link: Strong export growth and the oil-import shock from Middle East supply disruption affect the yen (already at 159.50/USD) and the Nikkei; the GDP contraction may shape BoJ rate expectations.

key_facts: U.K. inflation rose to 3.6% in the 12 months to October, up from 3.5% in September and the highest level in a year; the reading was in line with economists polled by Reuters.
Motor fuel costs were the largest contributor, rising 33.2% year-on-year, the largest one-year rise since July 2022.

The average petrol price rose by 5.2 pence per liter between September and October to 174.7 pence per liter, the highest since Aug. 2022; diesel rose by 7 pence per liter to 199.5 pence per liter, the highest since ONS records began in 1996.

Since the U.S.-Iran war began in late February, inflation has risen sharply after a brief dip thanks to an energy price cap revised upward in July; oil prices have retreated from wartime highs above $100 a barrel but remain elevated.

key_facts: The U.S. Commerce Department's interim rule, released Monday, requires data centers in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia to obtain a U.S. government license to purchase advanced AI chips, including Nvidia's. Facilities already serving large Chinese customers have 90 days to apply for a license or face future export restrictions.

About 75% of China's overseas AI compute was forecast to be concentrated in Southeast Asia by end-2026, per October estimates from the Institute for Progress. Malaysia is seen as most exposed; Capital Economics estimates the restrictions could knock 0.2 percentage points off Malaysia's GDP growth forecasts through 2028.

The rule exempts U.S.-linked firms, which analysts say could let Chinese companies keep renting advanced compute via U.S. cloud providers, including data centers in Virginia. Oracle canceled a multibillion-dollar chip-leasing deal with Tencent in early November, per the Financial Times.
